# Problem

Welche Standards gelten fuer das Dokumentieren von Design-Entscheidungen: wann muss eine Entscheidung dokumentiert werden und was muss der Eintrag enthalten?

# Lösung

Design-Entscheidungen werden ausschliesslich als Tickets in dieser Wissensdatenbank dokumentiert, nie in CLAUDE.md oder design.md-Dateien. Dokumentationspflichtig ist eine Entscheidung, wenn mindestens eines zutrifft: (1) es wurde zwischen zwei oder mehr sinnvollen Ansaetzen gewaehlt, (2) die Wahl beeinflusst Architektur oder zukuenftige Erweiterbarkeit, (3) ein spaeterer Leser koennte sich fragen warum wurde das so gemacht. Jeder Eintrag muss enthalten: die getroffene Entscheidung, die erwogenen Alternativen, Pro und Contra je Alternative sowie die Begruendung der Wahl - eine Entscheidung ohne Begruendung ist beim naechsten abweichenden Fall wertlos. Naheliegende, aber verworfene Ansaetze immer kurz mit Grund der Verwerfung nennen. Beispiel-Struktur: Entscheidung Node-Graph statt Fixed-Grid fuer Navigation - Node-Graph pro: flexibel bei irregulaerem Terrain, contra: aufwaendiger aufzubauen; Fixed-Grid pro: simpel und schneller Lookup, contra: Speicherverschwendung bei leerem Raum und schlechte Diagonalen - gewaehlt wurde der Node-Graph, weil das Terrain stark irregulaer ist.

# Problem

Does the parser survive the player's apostrophe, parens (like this) and a comma?

# Lösung

Yes if it does: contains don't, 3x4 and a dash - here.

# Problem

Which scale factor should the Euclidean A* heuristic use in MeshPathfinder, and why does 10.0 produce non-optimal paths?

# Lösung

Decision: scale factor 9.0. Alternatives: scale 10.0 (original) pro: faster search, closer to actual cost; contra: inadmissible for diagonal moves because 10*sqrt(2)=14.14 exceeds the cheapest diagonal cost of 13, so paths are non-optimal. Scale 9.0 (chosen) pro: admissible since 9*sqrt(2)=12.73 < 13, guarantees optimal paths; contra: slightly more nodes explored. Octile distance pro: perfectly tight admissible bound; contra: more complex to implement, gains marginal. Rationale: 9.0 is the largest integer scale that remains admissible given the cheapest diagonal move cost (10 base + 3 diagonal = 13). Simple change with guaranteed optimality.

# Problem

Why does the A* search miss better paths when a node is rediscovered with a lower cost, and how is the open set managed?

# Lösung

Decision: use lazy deletion with a closed set instead of open-set tracking. Alternatives: open-set tracker (original) pro: no duplicate records; contra: cannot update the priority of nodes already in the queue, so better paths are missed. Lazy deletion plus closed set (chosen) pro: always uses the best fCost, handles re-discovery correctly; contra: slightly larger priority queue from duplicates. Decrease-key with an indexed priority queue pro: optimal queue size; contra: Java PriorityQueue does not support decrease-key, would require a custom PQ. Rationale: lazy deletion fixes the correctness issue (stale priorities) with minimal code change, and the closed set prevents reprocessing. Standard pattern for A* in Java.

# Problem

Why do HashMap lookups with MeshNode keys fail when different instances share the same coordinates?

# Lösung

Decision: implement equals() and hashCode() based on the (x, y, z) coordinates. Alternatives: reference identity (original) pro: nothing to implement; contra: breaks HashMap lookups if different MeshNode instances share coordinates, a fragile assumption. Coordinate equality (chosen) pro: correct HashMap behaviour, safe to create MeshNode instances anywhere; contra: coordinates must uniquely identify a node within a mesh. Rationale: MeshNode is used as a HashMap key in MeshPathfinder (gScore, cameFrom) and compared via equals() in tests and path reconstruction. Reference identity worked by accident but was a latent bug.

# Problem

Why was the 4.5-block diagonal drop limit dead code, with drops capped at 4.0 instead?

# Lösung

Decision: check the drop distance (4.5 limit) before the same-level/step-up distance (4.0 limit). Alternatives: check dy >= -1 first (original) pro: simpler order; contra: the dy > 0 check at 4.5 was dead code, drops were capped at 4.0. Check dy > 0 first (chosen) pro: both limits apply correctly, 4.5 for drops and 4.0 for flat/step-up; contra: slightly less obvious order. Rationale: drops-first matches the original intent that drops should allow 4.5 diagonal distance. The more specific condition must be checked before the more general one.

# Problem

Why does the bot turn around on the target block after landing instead of simply stopping where it lands?

# Lösung

Decision: the final path node counts as reached when the player is on the ground within FINAL_ARRIVAL_RADIUS (0.5) of the true block center, with the per-node random target offset excluded, and horizontal speed is at most FINAL_ARRIVAL_MAX_SPEED (0.12 b/t). Intermediate nodes keep the tight sphere (0.18 against the offset target) or the in-bounds box check. Alternatives: tight sphere only (original) pro: guarantees a centered stop comfortably inside the 0.6 test arrival radius; contra: the bot lands off-center (jumps always do, and the walk target itself sits up to 0.25 off-center from the random offset) and then walks the last fraction of a block, at which point the desired yaw flips sign whenever the player oversteps and the overshoot logic spins him back - the reported turning around the block center after landing. Box check for the final node too pro: simplest unification; contra: triggers up to 0.65 from center, outside the downstream 0.6 test radius, and standing half-off the block edge is not a finished-looking stop. 0.5 true-center radius plus low-speed gate (chosen) pro: fires the moment the bot stands securely on the block, covering every normal landing and the offset walk target so no re-centering walk ever starts, and the whole 0.5 disc counts as arrived so the yaw-flip pirouette cannot occur; contra: the resting point varies by up to 0.5 from center, which is exactly the human-looking outcome and is tolerated by all downstream checks (tests 0.6, WalkTravelMethod 2 blocks, bot reach 4.0). Velocity-projected arrival pro: theoretically earliest stop; contra: predicting the friction slide duplicates physics the brake logic already handles. Rationale: the pirouette is purely a product of chasing a sub-0.25-block point - widening arrived to the area a human would consider being on the block makes the pathological geometry disappear, while the speed gate preserves the only thing the tight stop actually protected, not sliding off the far edge. See also [[STR-007]] and [[STR-013]].

# Problem

The camera still orbits the target for a few ticks between landing and the arrival speed gate opening - why does the arrival disc plus speed gate alone not remove the pirouette?

# Lösung

Decision: when on the ground inside the arrival disc while the speed gate is still closed, skip target steering entirely - hold the camera yaw (updateYaw(getYaw()), so the spring just settles) and run the same 8-way applyCounterBrake the landing brake uses, until the gate opens and arrival fires. Evidence: per-tick camera traces showed that during the 1-4 ticks between landing (speed 0.15-0.26) and the gate opening (at most 0.12) the normal movement logic kept steering toward the walk target. Standing next to the point, the desired yaw orbited it at roughly 7 deg per tick (desiredYaw -150.7 then -143.5 then -136.5 then -125.7 over four ticks at a constant 0.2 speed) and the camera followed. The S-only shouldBrake path pushes opposite the view, which points at the target, so the sideways momentum component was never killed and the orbit persisted. Verified by trace afterwards: zero remaining ticks of target-steering inside the disc, and the camera yaw stays constant through landing and stop. See also [[STR-006]] and [[STR-008]].

# Problem

Why does the bot whip its camera around to face the travel direction just to brake after a jump landing?

# Lösung

Decision: during the active landing brake (speed above 0.1 b/t after a jump landing) the camera keeps turning smoothly toward the next path target via camera.updateYaw with no snap, and the residual momentum is countered with movement keys - the momentum direction relative to the current view yaw is quantized to the 8 key directions (max 22.5 deg error) and the opposing combo is pressed: S when the momentum runs forward, A/D counter-strafe when it runs sideways, W when it runs backward, diagonals combined. Alternatives: snapYaw(velocityYaw) plus press S (original) pro: brake force exactly antiparallel to momentum, fastest possible deceleration; contra: the camera visibly whips around to face the travel direction just to brake and then has to turn back, reported as the bot turning around to brake instead of just pressing S - an instant yaw snap plus an unmotivated turn is a double bot-tell. Keep the view on target and always press S pro: single-key simplicity, no snap; contra: S pushes opposite the view, not opposite the momentum, so after diagonal jumps or mid-turn the momentum can run sideways to the view, S then barely decelerates (cos near 0 at 90 deg) and adds a sideways push that can shove the player off a single-block platform. 8-way key counter-brake with smooth view (chosen) pro: reads exactly like a player braking with eyes already on the next target, worst-case key misalignment is 22.5 deg so at least 92 percent of the push still decelerates; contra: slightly weaker than a perfect antiparallel brake, up to 38 percent of the push acts sideways for a few ticks, verified against the single-block corner tests. 4-way quantization pro: simpler sector logic; contra: max misalignment 45 deg, only about 71 percent decelerates and up to 71 percent acts sideways, measurably worse on single-block landings for no readability gain. Rationale: the brake purpose - kill momentum before the next segment - survives quantization, while the camera behaviour, the only part the user actually sees, becomes indistinguishable from a player: gaze on the next target, fingers doing the braking.

# Problem

After mining a wall the next A* path still ignores the hole and drives the bot back through the cleared section - when is the chunk mesh invalidated?

# Lösung

Decision: LevelChunkMixin.setBlockState invalidates the mesh for the chunk via MeshManager.invalidateMesh(chunkCoord) whenever the change flips air to solid or back, the chunk level is the client one, and at least one entity has a mesh for that chunk. Alternatives: empty mixin with no invalidation (original) pro: simple, no perf cost; contra: mining a wall leaves the mesh thinking the wall is still solid, the next A* search finds a path that ignores the hole the bot just dug, and PathWalker drives the bot back through the no-longer-walkable section. Per-block slice update pro: cheap per update; contra: tricky to get right because a single block change can affect not just its own column but every neighbour reachability (line-of-sight checks span 5 blocks either way), so the bug surface is high while full regen is correctness-first. Full chunk regen on every block update without a filter pro: trivially correct; contra: every redstone tick, leaf decay and waterlogged toggle would re-walk the entire 16x16 chunk and tests would slow to a crawl. Full chunk regen filtered to air/solid flips plus active-mesh plus client-side (chosen) pro: three short and cheap conditions prune the expensive call to the cases where it matters, non-mesh chunks pay nothing, and the level filter prevents the double-fire in single-player; contra: sub-state edits that do affect walkability, such as a stair direction change altering the upper face slope, are not currently detected - not a problem in practice since bots do not navigate stairs as a special case yet. Lazy dirty flag with regen on next access pro: avoids work for chunks not currently queried; contra: adds a flag to track and a check on every findOrBuildNearestNode call, and the current filters already make eager regen affordable. Rationale: the filters reduce the firing rate by more than 100x since most setBlockState calls are sub-state edits or in chunks no bot is using, a 16x16 walk is sub-millisecond when it does fire, and the resulting mesh is guaranteed consistent with what the client sees. The lazy-flag option remains available if profiling later shows a bottleneck.

# Problem

The bot walks perfectly on the line between nodes and reads as a bot - how is lateral drift added without breaking precise jumps?

# Lösung

Decision: PathWalker injects brief 1-2 tick sideways key presses (left/right) on path segments where the current and next-two nodes are same-Y gap=1, a corridor, with a 40-80 tick cooldown between strafes, disabled on any non-corridor segment. Alternatives: no strafing (state before the change) pro: most predictable movement; contra: every walking step is on the perfect line between nodes, with no lateral drift like a human hand on the keyboard. Continuous low-amplitude strafing on all segments pro: most humanness; contra: single-block-platform jumps need precise alignment, a strafe in flight pushes the player off the landing block and tests fail. Strafe only on safe corridors in brief windows with cooldown (chosen) pro: drifts the bot off-line by about 0.1 blocks on corridors where the alignment-hold and spring camera absorb it, and never touches jump-prep or in-air segments; contra: adds keyLeft/keyRight to the applyMovement surface, and calls during retreat or brake must explicitly pass strafeDir=0. Strafe via random target-offset perturbation pro: no new key state; contra: the existing target offset of 0.05-0.25 blocks already provides micro-variance on the target, whereas strafing varies the input, which is what reads as an imperfect human keyboard hand. Rationale: the isSafeCorridor predicate reliably excludes the failure modes - jumps, sharp turns, retreats - while still firing on the segments where a viewer is most likely to notice the missing drift. applyMovement now explicitly drives all six movement keys so any in-flight strafe is cleared whenever a non-strafing path (jump, brake, retreat) calls it with strafeDir=0. See also [[STR-011]].

# Problem

The vertical aim is identical every tick during walks and reads as a frozen bot gaze - how is pitch variance added without delaying jumps?

# Lösung

Decision: while straightWalkTicks is above 20, the bot is on the ground, not approaching a jump, and the target is more than 1.5 blocks away, add a slowly-refreshing offset (2.5 deg Gaussian either way, refreshed every 20-40 ticks) to the desired pitch passed into CameraController.updatePitch. Outside those conditions the offset is zeroed so the next walk starts clean. Alternatives: no pitch variance (state before the change) pro: most predictable, pitch always near horizontal; contra: frozen gaze, the vertical aim is identical every tick of every walk and reads as bot. Continuous pitch noise pro: most lively; contra: when approaching a jump the pitch is part of the camera-derived facing target, so noisy pitch makes the JUMP_FACING_TOLERANCE_DEG angular check flutter and can delay a jump by 1-2 ticks, manifesting as occasional stuck at the edge. Gated low-frequency offset (chosen) pro: the 20-tick straight-walk gate guarantees the bot is well past any jump prep, the 1.5-block target distance gate excludes the precise approach, and because the offset is part of the desired pitch the spring-damper does the smoothing so the output is a slow drift rather than jitter; contra: the offset must be zeroed on exit, and failing to do so would leave the next jump approach with a stale tilt. Rationale: pitch variance is a scanning-the-path cue that only makes sense during sustained walking. The straight-walk counter is shared with micro-strafing for the same reason - once the bot is committed to a long straight run, both humanness effects activate together. See also [[STR-010]].

# Problem

Long jumps fire instantly the moment conditions align and read as a script - where should a pre-jump pause go?

# Lösung

Decision: when entering the gap of 5 or more retreat branch from a standstill (forwardVel at most 0.14), pause for a Gaussian 4-12 tick window (mean 7, sigma 2) before starting the retreat. The camera continues aiming at the target during the pause and no movement keys are pressed. If the bot enters with sprint-speed velocity (forwardVel above 0.14, meaning the standard skip-retreat branch applies), the hesitation is skipped as well. Alternatives: no hesitation (state before the change) pro: fastest jump execution; contra: long jumps fire instantly when conditions align and read as a script, whereas a human pauses to look at a 4-air-block gap before committing. Hesitation on all jumps from gap 2 upward pro: most consistent humanness; contra: adds 250-500 ms to every step-up and short jump, chain-jumps over single-block platforms get visibly choppy, and tests relying on a continuous gap=2 chain regress. Hesitation on gap 5 or more gated to a standstill (chosen) pro: targets exactly the situation a viewer notices, the bot facing a wide gap and stopping to pre-aim, while mid-stride entries that are already sprinting do not pause so smooth gap-2 chains are preserved; contra: adds roughly 250-500 ms per max-range jump. Look-then-pause via camera-only state pro: hesitation visible without halting movement; contra: the retreat phase needs the bot still, and entering retreat at speed risks falling off the back edge - stopping is the correct mechanic regardless of humanness. Rationale: it matches the visual cue a human gives at a long jump and is mechanically aligned with the retreat phase, which already requires the bot to stop. Realised in the same if (maxJumpPhase == 0) branch, sharing its state.

# Problem

The camera whips around when the player steps past a path node at very short range - why does the desired yaw flip by up to 180 degrees?

# Lösung

Decision: stableDesiredYaw(aimDx, aimDz) returns the atan2 yaw toward the aim vector but freezes at its last stable value while the horizontal distance is below 0.5 blocks. It is used for the main movement desired-yaw and for the landing-brake retarget, and is reset on start(). Alternatives: raw atan2 every tick (original) pro: no state; contra: within about 0.5 blocks of a node, stepping past the point flips the yaw target by up to 180 deg between ticks, and the camera whips after every flip - a fast sweep with the velocity cap, a snap without it. This happens at overflown intermediate nodes where airborne advance is denied at sharp turns, during landing-brake slides toward a close node, and it was the engine of the post-landing pirouette. Freeze below 0.5 blocks (chosen) pro: the gaze keeps its last meaningful direction through the unstable zone, node advance or genuine separation resets it naturally, and it costs one float plus one boolean of state; contra: while frozen the gaze can be slightly stale if the player drifts sideways, which is irrelevant at sub-half-block range where any direction reads as looking at the node. Slerp or low-pass on the desired yaw pro: smooths flips too; contra: adds lag to all target changes including legitimate course corrections, whereas the instability is strictly a near-field problem so a distance gate is the precise tool. Rationale: the yaw target is simply not meaningful information at sub-half-block range - any human looks at the block underfoot without re-aiming at its mathematical center point. See also [[STR-006]] and [[STR-007]].

# Problem

EnderPearl tests flake under accelerated ticks because the throw is rejected - where should the item cooldown be waited out?

# Lösung

Decision: EnderPearlTests waits on the client-side ItemCooldowns, synced from the server via ClientboundCooldownPacket, and then adds a 30-tick safety margin before calling EnderPearlTravelMethod.start(). The travel method itself does not check or clear the cooldown. Alternatives: a fixed waitTicks(N) larger than 20 only pro: simple; contra: non-deterministic under accelerated ticks, different -PtickSpeed values need different N. Poll the cooldown in test setup plus a 30-tick safety margin (chosen) pro: deterministic on the client side, authoritative because it is server-synced via packet, and it scales with any tick rate while the margin absorbs client/server tick-rate drift; contra: tests must know to poll, which couples the test to the cooldown mechanic. Check the cooldown inside EnderPearlTravelMethod.tickThrowing pro: encapsulated; contra: a compensating wrapper around a test-harness ordering issue, and the method should not silently delay callers who asked for a throw. Rationale: the travel method correctly fails when a throw is ignored, so the test setup phase is the right place to establish preconditions. The 30-tick safety margin handles client/server tick drift: the client ItemCooldowns can clear ahead of the server under -PtickSpeed above 1 when the frame rate outpaces the tick rate, and a client-side use press during that gap is silently rejected by the server. See also [[STR-015]].

# Problem

The ender pearl use press is silently rejected by the server and the travel method fails - how long must keyUse be held?

# Lösung

Decision: hold keyUse for 20 accelerated ticks before releasing in tickThrowing. Alternatives: hold for 2 ticks (original) pro: minimal; contra: a single use is rejected if rightClickDelay is above 0 from a prior use. Hold for 6 ticks pro: allows one retry after rightClickDelay expires; contra: still fails under accelerated ticks where client/server drift puts the first two attempts inside a lingering server-side cooldown window. Hold for 20 ticks (chosen) pro: gives 4-5 retry attempts and covers the server-side cooldown expiring mid-hold under accelerated ticks; contra: very slightly wastes ticks when the throw succeeds on the first attempt. Rationale: the server-side cooldown is 20 ticks and the client-side cooldown can clear up to that window before the server one at high -PtickSpeed values, so holding for 20 ticks guarantees at least one attempt hits a cooldown-clear server state. In practice only the first successful attempt throws a pearl, since subsequent presses are silently absorbed by the server fresh cooldown, so the hold does not multiply pearls. See also [[STR-014]].

# Problem

Should every consumer of the camera module be forced onto a world-space aim API, or is a low-level yaw/pitch API still needed?

# Lösung

Decision: expose two API tiers on CameraController - low-level (updateYaw, updatePitch, snapYaw) and high-level (aimAt(player, x, y, z), isAimedAt(player, x, y, z, tol)). Pathfinding stays on the low-level API, the bot uses the high-level one. Alternatives: two-tier API (chosen) pro: each consumer uses the tier that fits its data flow, and the camera module needs no knowledge of movement physics; contra: slightly larger surface area. Only the high-level aimAt pro: smallest surface, forces all yaw/pitch through one path; contra: PathWalker yaw targets come from movement physics (velocity yaw during retreat, velocity-facing during landing brake, path-direction yaw otherwise) rather than from a world point, so forcing aimAt would require pushing jump-decision, retreat and brake logic into the camera module or splatting it back out via extra variants. Only the low-level updateYaw/updatePitch pro: clean separation; contra: duplicates the derive yaw/pitch from a world point and write to player pattern across every consumer that aims at a block - the bot had this in 3 phases. Rationale: the duplication eliminated in the bot (3 phases of about 8 lines each) has a real cost, while forcing pathfinding onto aimAt would require the camera module to know about movement-physics concepts it should not.

# Problem

Should the camera spring physics parameters be runtime-configurable or hardcoded?

# Lösung

Decision: the spring physics parameters (TURN_ACCEL=0.8, TURN_FRICTION=0.8, PITCH_ACCEL=0.5, PITCH_FRICTION=0.7) are hardcoded constants in CameraController, not configurable at runtime. Alternatives: hardcoded constants (chosen) pro: simple, no config files, and the values are proven stable; contra: requires a code change to tune. Config file (camera.json) pro: tunable without recompile; contra: extra complexity and another config to manage. Passed from consumer config pro: flexible per consumer; contra: couples the camera module to the consumer config. Rationale: the values are well-tuned from extensive testing, and runtime tuning via config commands was removed to simplify the system. Per-target variation comes from the look-speed multiplier rather than from tunable constants, because multipliers are unit-less and easier to reason about than re-tuning the physics directly. See also [[STR-021]].

# Problem

Should CameraController be a static utility like PathWalker or an instance?

# Lösung

Decision: CameraController is instance-based (non-static). Alternatives: instance-based (chosen) pro: multiple independent camera controllers, testable, no shared state; contra: requires a field to hold the instance. Static like PathWalker pro: simple access, no instantiation; contra: only one camera at a time, hard to test, and it couples consumers. Rationale: the goal is to support multiple automation systems (pathfinding, combat, mining) each with independent camera state.

# Problem

Should AngleUtil.isFacingTarget read its tolerance from a config or take it as a parameter?

# Lösung

Decision: AngleUtil.isFacingTarget takes the tolerance as a parameter instead of reading from a config. Alternatives: tolerance as a parameter (chosen) pro: flexible, no coupling to any config, reusable; contra: the caller must pass a value. Read from the CameraController config pro: encapsulated; contra: ties the utility to a controller instance and makes it less reusable. Read from a global config pro: simple; contra: couples to a specific config and is unusable by other modules. Rationale: different contexts need different tolerances - gap=2 uses 18 degrees, gap of 3 or more uses 36 degrees, and step-ups use 45 degrees.

# Problem

How are micro-saccades added during sustained aim without breaking the convergence gate?

# Lösung

Decision: CameraController exposes setMicroSaccadesEnabled(boolean). When enabled it injects tiny target perturbations (0.5 deg yaw, 0.3 deg pitch, either way) refreshed every 6-22 ticks (Gaussian, mean 12). The perturbation is excluded from isAimedAt so saccades never break the convergence gate. Alternatives: per-tick offset inside the controller (chosen) pro: the spring-damper absorbs the jitter naturally, one toggle per consumer, no caller code change; contra: adds saccade-state fields to the controller even when unused. Caller computes the saccade and passes it via offsets pro: the controller stays simple; contra: every consumer would duplicate the saccade state machine, and saccades would also affect raycasts because the offset target moves, which matters when callers like the bot already pass jitter offsets for face aim. Random walk on yaw directly between updates pro: no target change needed; contra: fights the spring physics, because every direct write resets velocity and causes a visible jerk. Rationale: the spring-damper is the right place to absorb noise - feeding a perturbed target produces a smoothly tracked perturbation, while writing directly to yaw would always conflict with the spring. Excluding saccades from isAimedAt matters because the bot hit-result gate already validates separately whether the raycast lands on the target, so letting saccades make isAimedAt flicker would cause spurious gate reopens.

# Problem

How is per-target variance in look speed introduced without destabilising the spring?

# Lösung

Decision: CameraController.setLookSpeedMultiplier(double m) scales the spring acceleration on both yaw and pitch, while friction is held constant. The default is 1.0, which is critical damping on yaw. Alternatives: scale acceleration only (chosen) pro: a simple knob where m above 1 introduces mild overshoot and m below 1 slows convergence, both of which feel human, and it preserves the soft feel of the damper; contra: underdamping at high m could in theory oscillate, but the multiplier range of roughly 0.7-1.3 stays well within stable bounds. Scale both acceleration and friction pro: stays critically damped at every multiplier; contra: removes the variance of behaviour so every aim feels the same shape only faster or slower, losing the sometimes the camera overshoots a hair texture that reads as human. Replace constants per target pro: most flexibility; contra: couples consumers to physics, as they would have to know which values are stable. Rationale: the overshoot at m above 1 is exactly the human-like artefact wanted - a perfectly damped camera at every speed still feels like a machine, just at different speeds. The bot rolls m from lookSpeedMin/Max (default 0.7 to 1.3) per target. See also [[STR-017]].

# Problem

Should pitch use the same spring-damper physics as yaw, or keep the exponential decay?

# Lösung

Decision: both yaw and pitch use spring-damper physics, with pitch using gentler constants (PITCH_ACCEL=0.5, PITCH_FRICTION=0.7) than yaw (TURN_ACCEL=0.8, TURN_FRICTION=0.8). Alternatives: spring-damper on both (chosen) pro: one physics model gives the same feel on both axes, supports the look-speed multiplier and saccades uniformly, and mild overshoot reads as human; contra: pitch can ring slightly more than the old exponential at large deltas. Exponential on both pro: trivially stable, no oscillation; contra: loses the momentum feel, cannot overshoot, cannot carry a saccade, and is asymmetric with yaw. Keep the old asymmetry of spring yaw with exponential pitch pro: it is what existed; contra: a different feel on each axis is visible - a viewer can tell yaw is heavier than pitch - and the multiplier and saccade plumbing would need duplicate code paths. Rationale: a single physics model reduces the look-speed multiplier and saccade implementations to one branch instead of two; the asymmetry was visible on diagonal jumps where pitch tracked instantly while yaw still swept; and PathWalker only consumes the smoothed pitch via setXRot, which is cosmetic, so its jump correctness depends solely on yaw and a different pitch profile cannot break path tests. The gentler pitch constants keep vertical tracking calm so the camera does not feel jumpy on every small terrain step.

# Problem

Per-tick traces show the smooth camera producing 141 degrees of yaw in a single tick - why does the spring snap on large turns?

# Lösung

Decision: updateYaw clamps the yaw angular velocity to MAX_YAW_SPEED_DEG_PER_TICK of 35 deg per tick, scaled by the look-speed multiplier. Alternatives: uncapped spring (original) pro: mathematically clean, converges fastest; contra: the spring first tick after a target change covers TURN_ACCEL times delta, so for a 180 deg flip that is a 144 deg single-tick snap. Per-tick yaw traces during pathwalking showed 74-141 deg jumps at path starts, at landing-brake retargets, and whenever a near node atan2 target flipped: the spring only smooths small deltas, and for large ones it IS the snap it was meant to prevent. Lower TURN_ACCEL globally pro: no new constant; contra: slows every turn including small corrections, so jump-facing waits (18-36 deg tolerance) and the whole tuned movement physics shift, while the problem is only the first saturated ticks of large turns. Velocity cap scaled by the look-speed multiplier (chosen) pro: large turns become a constant-rate sweep of about 35 deg per tick, roughly 700 deg per second, which is a brisk visibly continuous mouse turn that eases out via the unchanged spring once the remaining delta is small, and small-delta behaviour is byte-identical while multiplier scaling keeps per-target speed variance alive during the saturated phase; contra: adds 2-4 ticks to 90-180 deg turns and jump-facing fires correspondingly later, verified against the full jump-timing test suite. Cap inside consumers pro: camera module untouched; contra: every consumer would duplicate the clamp, and the failure mode lives in the shared spring rather than in any one consumer. Rationale: measured traces showed the smooth camera producing 141 deg in one tick, and the cap converts exactly those ticks into a sweep while leaving all small-delta smoothing untouched, in the one place all consumers share. See also [[STR-013]].

# Problem

Where should long-running automation strategies like strip mining live, given that the task queue only holds one-shot entries?

# Lösung

Decision: specialized long-running automation (strip mining, future farming or building) lives in a layer above the task queue: BotBehavior (interface with id, start, tick returning BehaviorStatus, abort, statusLine) plus a static BehaviorRunner (registry, one active behavior, ticked from the bot module before BotController.tick). Behaviors plan by enqueuing BotTasks and waiting for the controller to go idle; they never simulate input themselves. Specialized modules such as modules/miner depend on the bot module and register their behaviors at init, the same registry pattern as the pathfinding TravelMethod and Navigator. Alternatives: grow BotController phases per use-case pro: no new layer; contra: the controller phases encode how to interact with one block humanly, so mixing in what to mine next over minutes would bloat the project most delicate class and every new use-case would touch the same file. Meta-tasks in the queue extending the GatherAreaTask pattern pro: reuses the queue; contra: a queue entry is consumed once, while strategies need to observe results and re-plan (scan, mine, verify, scan) - GatherAreaTask already shows the limit since it can only pre-plan a static snapshot. Each module registers its own ClientTick hook and drives BotController ad-hoc pro: no bot-module change; contra: two modules could fight over the controller with no arbitration, there would be no shared stop semantics so /bot stop could not stop them, and no discoverability or status. Behavior layer with registry and a single active slot (chosen) pro: strategy and execution separate cleanly, behaviors own what and where next while the controller owns the human-like how, one active behavior gives natural arbitration, /bot stop stops top-down from runner to controller, and the registry pattern is already proven in this codebase; contra: one more concept and tick hook in the bot module. Rationale: the miner immediately needed observe-replan loops (verify each step, chase ore veins, fail fast on hazards) that neither the controller phases nor one-shot queue entries can express, and the next specialized modules get the same seam for free.

# Problem

Should the camera freeze during a reaction delay, and why does freezing read as stop-motion?

# Lösung

Decision: while a deferred-action reaction delay is in flight, the bot camera keeps easing toward its last aim point - aimCameraAt records the point and the deferred gate replays it each tick. Movement keys stay released, but the gaze finishes its swing and keeps saccading. Alternatives: freeze everything during the delay (original) pro: simplest, and the pause is clearly visible; contra: the spring-damper camera can be mid-swing when the delay starts, since SCANNING 15 deg facing tolerance fires while the camera still has high angular velocity, so halting the turn for 1-10 ticks and then resuming reads as stop-motion, the opposite of the humanness the delay exists for. Ease toward the last aim point during the delay (chosen) pro: the body pauses with movement released while the gaze settles naturally, exactly what a human pausing between deciding and acting looks like, and saccades stay alive; contra: one extra static field set (lastAim) on every camera-driving tick. Only delay transitions where the camera has converged pro: no mid-swing freeze possible; contra: couples delay placement to camera state, and SCANNING to NAVIGATING with its 15 deg tolerance is precisely the transition where the beat is most visible and most wanted. Rationale: the reaction delay models a decision pause, not a motor freeze - humans stop walking while they think, but their eyes finish settling on the target. See also [[STR-042]].

# Problem

There is no smooth transition between tasks - the bot stands still for 60 ticks after every block break when more work is queued. Why?

# Lösung

Decision: when walkAfterCollect is set and taskQueue.peek() is not null, COLLECTING exits as soon as items are absent, bypassing the standard itemAbsenceTicks 60-tick sustained-absence window. When no further task is queued the original sustained-absence window applies. Companion change: if the bot ends up within reach of the next task by the time COLLECTING exits, for example the next ore in a vein right next to the one just mined, skip SCANNING and transition straight to LOOKING, because the aim cue is unnecessary when there is no movement to do. Alternatives: always wait itemAbsenceTicks (original) pro: tolerates transient absence between sequentially spawning drops; contra: adds a visible 60-tick pause after every block break in a multi-target flow, reported as no fluid transition between tasks. Walk toward the next task during COLLECTING (first attempt) pro: removes the pause and keeps the bot moving; contra: the walk is a dumb horizontal pursuit rather than PathWalker, so the bot bumps into the next target from the wrong angle, for example directly against the side of a tree trunk, and LOOKING then cannot establish line of sight so the chop-tree task fails with a look timeout - replacing the NAVIGATING standoff logic with a direct walk is wrong. Reduce itemAbsenceTicks globally pro: one-line change; contra: trades smoothness in multi-task flows against pickup reliability in single-task flows where multiple drops arrive in waves, and the 60-tick wait is the right answer for the single-task case. Skip the wait only when more work is queued (chosen) pro: a single surgical condition where queued-task flows get the immediate transition and single-task flows keep their robustness, with straggler drops on the walk path picked up by the 1.5-block vanilla radius during NAVIGATING; contra: the next task SCANNING to NAVIGATING sequence does the transition rather than continuing the walk, though the brief camera turn cue actually matches the human look where you are going pattern. Rationale: the itemAbsenceTicks wait solves a different problem (the multi-drop pickup race) than the smoothness complaint addresses (queue-driven multi-task flow); one window cannot satisfy both, and the queue gives a deterministic signal to switch. See also [[STR-026]].

# Problem

The bot walks through its drops staring straight ahead, and when it does track them it cranes its head further and further down - how should the COLLECTING gaze work?

# Lösung

Decision: during COLLECTING the camera aims at what the bot is doing - the nearest item while walking to it (walkToward takes the full 3D target), the item while standing in pickup range unless it is nearly underfoot (horizontal distance squared at most 0.5), lastMinedPos while waiting for the drop to sync, and the last aim point (still saccading) while waiting out the absence window. All drop-directed aims go through aimCollectGaze, where the downward pitch is capped at a per-phase angle drawn uniformly from collectGazePitchMinDeg to collectGazePitchMaxDeg (default 38-52 deg). When the direct angle to the item would exceed the cap, the aim point is pushed out along the same horizontal direction to the distance where the pitch equals the cap, keeping the same yaw so walk steering is unaffected while the gaze rests on the ground ahead. Micro-saccades are enabled for the whole phase. Alternatives: smooth yaw to walk direction only (original) pro: steers the walk correctly; contra: pitch stays frozen at whatever INTERACTING left, namely eye level at the mined block, so the bot walks through its drops staring ahead and stands dead still with a locked gaze during the 60-tick absence window - both read as bot. Aim at the item point directly (first attempt) pro: the gaze follows the drop; contra: the pitch steepens continuously on approach, about 22 deg at 4 blocks and about 58 deg at 1 block, so the head visibly cranes further down, which the user reported as unnatural - humans do not head-track a point on the floor, they hold a scanning angle. Aim at the item with pitch capped at a ground-scan angle (chosen) pro: far away the bot looks at the drop at a flat angle, and closing in it holds a steady scanning the floor ahead posture while the drop enters the lower view, with per-phase variance of 38-52 deg avoiding a fixed signature angle and yaw unchanged so walking is unaffected; contra: the gaze passes over items closer than the cap distance of about 1.4 blocks, which is acceptable since vanilla pickup needs no aim and this is exactly the floor-scan look requested. Fixed 45 deg pitch during COLLECTING with no item tracking pro: simplest; contra: loses the distant-drop glance that makes the walk-over read intentional, and pins the pitch even when the drop is above eye level on a ledge, where looking up at it is the natural move - the cap only restricts downward pitch. Rationale: the walk steering needs item-directed yaw anyway, and capping only the downward pitch keeps both stories right: I see the drop over there at range, and I am scanning the ground in front of me up close.

# Problem

The bot aims at an invisible block face and burns the full look timeout - which face of a block should it target?

# Lösung

Decision: BlockInteractor.faceTowardPlayer sorts the up-to-three player-oriented faces by how directly they point at the eye and returns the first whose neighbour block is air; only when all candidates are covered does it fall back to the dominant face. Alternatives: dominant axis only (original) pro: one comparison chain; contra: for a floor block right in front of the feet the dominant face is UP, since eye height is about 1.6 over a block roughly 1 away, but UP is still covered by the block above - the bot aims at an invisible face, the raycast hits the coverer, and the task burns the full lookTimeout before failing, observed as 11 look-timeout retries in a single miner test run while the strictly closer side face was visible the whole time. Exposed-face preference ordered by dominance (chosen) pro: picks the face a human would click, namely the most direct one that is actually visible, at a cost of three cheap isAir checks per call, and the destroy-packet direction hint improves consistently, with covered-everything falling back to dominance which callers resolve by clearing blockers first; contra: an air neighbour does not guarantee a clear ray from the eye since other blocks can still intersect the path, but the hit-result gate keeps protecting that case and the heuristic removes the common systematic failure. Full raycast per candidate face pro: exact visibility; contra: a level.clip per face per LOOKING tick for a case that three block reads already solve. Rationale: the dominant-axis bug was systematic, missing on first attempt for every floor-level block adjacent to the player, while the fix is local, cheap, and strictly more accurate as an estimate of which face can I see. See also [[STR-033]].

# Problem

The client shows air after a block break but the server reverted it and no drop ever spawned - how is a break confirmed?

# Lösung

Decision: INTERACTING requires two authoritative signals before transitioning out: a sustained-air window of CONFIG.airConfirmTicks consecutive ticks (default 8), and a drop entity existing within a 5x5x5 AABB around the target. Alternatives: single-tick isCurrentTargetComplete check (original) pro: minimal; contra: under accelerated ticks the client break prediction races ahead of the server, so the client shows air and the bot transitions while the server rejects and restores the block, and no drop spawns. Sustained-air window only pro: zero new infrastructure; contra: client-side sequenced-transaction prediction can hold the predicted-air state for a long time before the server revert ack arrives - under tickSpeed=20 an observed lastMinedPos state=iron_ore at COLLECTING exit proved the server never broke it, yet airConfirmTicks had fired, so no fixed window size is safe. Air plus drop entity (chosen) pro: the drop entity is authoritative because the server only spawns it after actually completing the break, so if the client air is a mere prediction the server later reverts, no drop entity ever appears and the bot keeps mining until maxBreakTicks - and it works independently of tick-rate jitter; contra: adds a per-tick AABB query once airConfirmTicks is satisfied, which is cheap for a 5x5x5 region, and for blocks that break with no drop such as wrong-tool breaks, INTERACTING runs to maxBreakTicks and fails the task, which is correct behaviour since no drop is useless anyway. Listen for ClientboundBlockUpdatePacket via mixin pro: authoritative; contra: requires a packet-pipeline mixin, while the drop-entity check uses an existing entity query of equivalent signal quality. Higher server tick rate to outpace the client pro: eliminates the race at the source; contra: can starve other server work and not all dev machines support it. Rationale: this is the first approach that is load-independent. Earlier attempts at tuning windows (3, 8, 16, 32, 48 ticks for airConfirmTicks or toolSettleTicks) passed in some runs and flaked in others depending on system load, whereas the drop-entity check relies on an actual server-side artifact rather than a timing assumption - the block broke if and only if the drop exists. See also [[STR-031]] and [[STR-044]].

# Problem

The bot keeps punching an already-broken block for 400 ticks when standing right next to it - why does the drop-entity check miss the drop?

# Lösung

Decision: poll the drop AABB on every INTERACTING tick and latch the result (dropSeenThisBreak) so a drop that exists for even one tick counts, and additionally accept growth of the main-inventory item count since break start as an alternative artifact. Evidence and problem: the original implementation queried the drop AABB only once the sustained-air window was already satisfied. That has a hole when the bot stands right next to the block, as in gallery mining or close-range re-approach: vanilla pickup inhales the drop within a tick of spawning, so no post-air query ever sees it, and the bot then kept attacking the already-broken block for the full maxBreakTicks - 400 ticks, which is 20 seconds of punching air in real time, with timestamped task-fail logs showing five such 400-tick stalls in one run. Why the inventory-growth signal is valid: the pickup itself is server-driven via slot sync, so it proves the break as authoritatively as the entity did. Risk assessment: a false positive would need the client air prediction plus an unrelated simultaneous pickup, and if the server then reverts, the planner verify step sees the solid block and re-plans, so the failure stays contained. See also [[STR-030]].

# Problem

The bot starts mining before it is actually aiming at the right block, or keeps staring after the crosshair is already on it - what gates LOOKING to INTERACTING?

# Lösung

Decision: LOOKING transitions to INTERACTING the moment mc.hitResult is a BlockHitResult and its getBlockPos() equals the target, meaning the client raycast points at the target block. There is no angular-convergence requirement, and the camera keeps easing toward its aim point during INTERACTING. The pre-attack hesitation still sits between the gate firing and the first attack. There is also no cosmetic settle countdown after aim, and the tool-settle wait that used to open INTERACTING is gone, replaced by selecting the tool during LOOKING - the carried-item packet travels to the server in parallel with the smooth camera turn, and INTERACTING calls resendCarriedItem once on tick 1 as a dropped-packet safety net. Alternatives: angular tolerance only (original) pro: simple; contra: when an obstacle sits in the line of sight the camera can be within tolerance of the target vector while the raycast lands on the obstacle, so the bot transitions and visibly starts attacking the wrong block. Angular plus hit-result (previous) pro: hit-result is authoritative while the angular check throttles polling; contra: the angular gate delays the attack past the moment a human would click, since the crosshair is already on the block but the bot keeps staring until the camera is within 5 deg of the ideal aim point, and the throttle argument is void because mc.hitResult is a field read. Hit-result only (chosen) pro: fires exactly when a human would click, as the crosshair touches the block, with obstacle correctness living entirely in the hit-result check so a raycast on an obstacle holds the gate and lookTimeout fails cleanly, proven by the mine-blocked-by-obstacle test; contra: the carried-item packet window shrinks when the crosshair is already near the target at LOOKING entry, covered by the per-tick resend in LOOKING, the defensive resend on INTERACTING tick 1, and the fact that the server only computes drops at break completion several ticks later. Server-side reach check pro: authoritative; contra: rejection is silent and arrives after the visible mis-aim, addressing neither reported symptom. Rationale: both reported symptoms bracket the same truth - the crosshair-on-block raycast, not camera convergence, is when mining should begin, and the angular gate added latency without adding correctness once the hit-result check existed. See also [[STR-033]], [[STR-034]] and [[STR-041]].

# Problem

With hit-result gating in place the bot locks up in LOOKING when mining a block in the middle of a stack - where should it aim?

# Lösung

Decision: aim at the center of the face most directly visible from the bot eye, computed via BlockInteractor.faceTowardPlayer, instead of the block center. Problem: with hit-result gating in place, aiming at the block center became unworkable for blocks in the middle of a stack, for example mining a tree from top to bottom. The center of the top log sits behind the lower log near face from the bot perspective, so a raycast aimed at the center lands on the lower log and the hit-result gate locks the bot in LOOKING until lookTimeout. Why the face aim works: the aim point shifts by 0.5 either way along the face-normal axis, so the raycast clears intermediate blocks and lands on the target. faceTowardPlayer already picks the same dominant-axis face used in the destroy packet, so no new concept is introduced. See also [[STR-032]] and [[STR-029]].

# Problem

The bot does not start mining even when it looks at the right block - why does human-aim jitter break the hit-result gate?

# Lösung

Decision: human-aim offsets are still applied, but only on the two axes perpendicular to the face normal - the jitter is clamped to the face plane. Problem: adding an offset along the face normal pushes the aim point off the face plane, so the raycast exits the block face range by the offset amount and just barely grazes a neighbour, or the platform below a single block. The hit-result gate then sees the neighbour and the bot stares forever, reported as the bot does not start mining even when it looks at the right block. Rationale: restricting the jitter to the in-face axes keeps the visual humanization while guaranteeing the aim ray crosses the target face rather than skirting it. See also [[STR-032]] and [[STR-033]].

# Problem

A target that is in reach but has no line of sight fails forever with repeated look timeouts at identical positions - what should happen on a look timeout?

# Lösung

Decision: when LOOKING times out, meaning the crosshair raycast never reached the target, the first timeout per target does not fail the task - it sets forceApproach and transitions to POSITIONING, which walks until the player is within APPROACH_CLOSE_DISTANCE (2.0) of the target instead of stopping at reach distance, then retries LOOKING. The second timeout fails with diagnostics covering position, chosen face and actual hitResult. Companion change: waiting out the full lookTimeout (40 ticks, 2 s at real speed) before re-approaching reads as staring, so once the camera has settled on its aim point (angular at most 3 deg) and the crosshair has rested on the same wrong block for WRONG_HIT_STREAK_TICKS (8) consecutive ticks, the geometry is not going to change and the re-approach fires immediately; the full timeout remains the fallback for non-block hit results such as sky, and as the second, failing attempt. Alternatives: fail on the first look timeout (original) pro: simple; contra: the controller had no in reach but no line of sight so move path, because POSITIONING stops at reach distance 4, so a target visible only from close up - for example a gallery block below eye level whose ceiling blocks the ray from a staircase ledge - failed forever no matter how often the planner retried, observed as repeated look timeouts at identical player positions in the miner. A human just steps closer. Re-approach once then fail (chosen) pro: fixes the systematic viewpoint problem for every consumer including bot commands and behaviors, and is bounded to one extra POSITIONING walk per target with the second timeout still failing cleanly, while the obstacle-blocked case keeps failing since walking into the wall never reaches close range; contra: adds roughly 40-100 ticks before a genuinely impossible target fails. Planner-side position gates, tried in the miner first pro: no controller change; contra: whack-a-mole, because the player position at plan time differs from execution time due to collect-walks and edge-standing on stair lips, so the planner cannot guarantee the viewpoint - the execution layer is the only place that knows the look failed. Raycast visibility pre-check before enqueuing pro: catches it earlier; contra: duplicates what LOOKING already discovers, and the answer to from where still requires moving, which is exactly the re-approach. Rationale: step closer when you cannot see it is both the human behavior and the only fix that works at the layer where visibility is actually determined. See also [[STR-050]].

# Problem

Every pause the bot makes is 1-10 ticks, so over minutes the cadence is recognizably machine-constant - where should longer pauses go?

# Lösung

Decision: the reaction delay at the SCANNING to NAVIGATING transition is drawn via HumanBehavior.randomTaskSwitchDelayTicks - with probability longPauseChance (default 0.04) a uniform breather pause of longPauseMinTicks to longPauseMaxTicks (default 12-25 ticks) replaces the standard Gaussian reaction delay. Other transitions keep the standard delay. Alternatives: no long pauses (original) pro: no test-budget impact; contra: every pause is 1-10 ticks so the cadence is recognizably machine-constant over minutes of watching, and the module description had promised pause patterns since the start while only the per-transition Gaussian existed. Long-pause chance on every scheduleAction pro: most variety; contra: multiplies the flake risk in tick-budgeted tests, since the within-reach vein flow alone rolls twice or more per run, and a mid-vein stall reads less natural than a pre-walk one. Long-pause chance only at SCANNING to NAVIGATING (chosen) pro: the spotted it, about to walk over moment is where humans genuinely idle by re-gripping the mouse or glancing at inventory, and walk-flow tests have the largest timeout budgets of 200-280 ticks so a rare extra 25 ticks fits; contra: the breather never occurs while standing in a vein, which is acceptable since the pre-attack hesitation and reaction delays already vary that cadence. Idle fidgeting with random look-arounds while IDLE pro: strongest idle realism; contra: IDLE means no task, which is out of scope for task-execution humanness and can be layered later. Rationale: applying it at a single transition gives a visible cadence-breaker with bounded, testable timing risk. The defaults are deliberately conservative at 4 percent and at most 25 ticks, and both knobs are config-exposed. See also [[STR-042]].

# Problem

The bot visibly zigzags across an area because tasks run in scan order - how is the next task chosen?

# Lösung

Decision: whenever the bot takes the next task from the queue - in startNextTask, the within-reach continuation in tickInteracting, and the walk-flow exit in tickCollecting - it takes the task whose target is nearest to the player current position via TaskQueue.pollNearest and peekNearest, with ties keeping insertion order, instead of the queue head. Explicit single commands still run in submission order, since a single-element queue is unaffected. Alternatives: FIFO in scan order (original) pro: deterministic and trivial; contra: BlockScanner sorts by distance to the scan center, so equidistant targets on opposite sides interleave and the bot visibly zigzags across the area, which no human does, and the order also ignores where the bot ends up after each task. Re-sort the whole queue after every task pro: same routing result; contra: mutates global order on every poll for no benefit over picking one element, and is harder to reason about with concurrent enqueues. Greedy nearest from the current position (chosen) pro: matches how a player works an area by finishing here and doing the closest thing next, at O(n) per poll over a small queue, with ties preserving FIFO so single-task flows and equal-distance tests stay deterministic; contra: greedy is not the globally optimal route, which is fine because humans are not optimal either. Nearest with a random second choice to model human suboptimality pro: models human imperfection; contra: deliberately re-introduces the zigzag the change removes, and randomness in route choice, as opposed to timing or aim, reads as erratic rather than human. Rationale: the visible failure mode was routing, and nearest-from-here is both the simplest fix and the most human-plausible heuristic.

# Problem

Path traces show the walk going straight at the target and then dog-legging sideways for the last two nodes - how is the standoff node chosen?

# Lösung

Decision: findStandoffNode scores candidate nodes that are in reach of the target by 1.05 times distToPlayer plus horizDistToTarget and takes the minimum. By the triangle inequality the sum is minimal for nodes on the straight player-to-target line, and the slight walk-distance bias makes the winner the first in-reach node on that line, which is also deterministic since all line nodes share the same raw sum and an unbiased score would fall back to hash iteration order. Alternatives: player-nearest in-reach node (original) pro: shortest walk; contra: regularly picks a node one block to the side of the approach line, whichever in-reach node happens to be closest to where the player stands, and debug path traces showed the walk going straight at the target and then dog-legging sideways for the last two nodes - the reported weird pathfinding in the ore-to-tree test. No human side-steps right before a target. Line-biased score (chosen) pro: walks read as straight at the target, stop in front of it, at the cost of one extra multiply per node; contra: the chosen node can be about 5 percent farther than the absolute nearest, which is irrelevant at reach distances. Target-nearest in-reach node pro: also line-ish; contra: walks past the natural stopping point right up to the block, which reads overeager and risks bumping into the target. Rationale: the dog-leg was a pure artifact of the scoring rather than of the mesh or A* - the path was the true shortest route to a badly chosen destination.

# Problem

PathWalker is launched for a 1.5-block two-node path whose first node is the player own position - when should navigation skip the pathfinding pipeline?

# Lösung

Decision: beginNavigation sends targets within reachDistance plus 2.5 blocks straight to POSITIONING, which walks at the target and hands over to LOOKING once in reach, instead of running standoff search plus A* plus PathWalker. Alternatives: always use the full pipeline (original) pro: one code path; contra: debug traces showed PathWalker launched for a 1.5-block two-node path whose first node was the player own position, incurring scan swing, reaction delay, walker start and final settling all for one step, which reads as mechanical orchestration where a player would just take two steps. POSITIONING shortcut for short hops (chosen) pro: the last-couple-blocks walk is literally what POSITIONING is - walk toward the target while looking at it and stop when in reach - so no new mechanics are needed; contra: POSITIONING walks blind without a mesh, which is fine for a couple of blocks on terrain the bot is already standing on, while longer routes keep the full pipeline. Raise reachDistance instead pro: even simpler; contra: changes mining semantics everywhere given server reach limits, and the problem is route ceremony rather than reach. Rationale: POSITIONING already implements the human behavior exactly, and the threshold keeps real navigation - drops, obstacles, distance - on the mesh pipeline.

# Problem

The bot mines with a bare hand and the task fails on timeout when the pickaxe is in inventory storage rather than the hotbar - what is the tool search scope?

# Lösung

Decision: InventoryHelper.selectBestTool scans all 36 main-inventory slots, hotbar plus 27 storage. When the best tool sits in storage (bestSlot 9 or higher) it is swapped into the currently selected hotbar slot via mc.gameMode.handleInventoryMouseClick with ClickType.SWAP before sending the carried-item packet. Alternatives: hotbar only, slots 0-8 (original) pro: minimal, one tight loop; contra: silently fails when the human-style carry tools in a row inventory has the pickaxe in storage, so the bot mines with a bare hand, no ore drops, and the task fails on the maxBreakTicks timeout - which looked like a robustness bug rather than a setup issue. Full inventory plus SWAP packet (chosen) pro: matches what a human player does by noticing the tool in storage, swapping it into the hotbar and mining, and the server-side hotbar held slot ends up with the right tool; contra: one extra container-click packet per tool select that needs swapping, which is small and idempotent, and the SWAP relies on inventoryMenu.containerId which is always valid for the player own inventory so no separate open inventory packet is needed. Move the tool via a direct items.set call pro: no packet; contra: client-only, so the server inventory diverges, the swapped item appears server-side in the original slot, and mining resolves against the wrong tool. Force-give the tool to the hotbar each tick pro: robust in creative; contra: does not work in survival and alters inventory state outside the test expectations. Rationale: full inventory plus SWAP is the cheapest correct answer - one packet the server natively understands, no inventory-state tricks and no creative-only assumptions. Slots 36-40, armor and offhand, are intentionally skipped since they are not tool slots in any practical sense, and the chosen hotbar destination is the currently selected slot so the carried-item packet needs no slot change afterwards. See also [[STR-043]].

# Problem

Removing the old settle delay made the transition to mining feel too eager - should the pause come back, and under which name?

# Lösung

Decision: after the LOOKING gate fires but before the first startAttack call, hold for a short uniform preAttackHesitation window (default 1-3 ticks, roughly 50-150 ms). During the window the camera keeps aiming and micro-saccades are enabled. This is a distinct concept from the removed settleDelay - it is humanness, not a timing buffer for packet sync. Alternatives: no pause at all, the state after the cleanup commit pro: fastest transition, reading as adjust then mine in one motion; contra: loses the visible human commit moment between locking on and clicking, and combined with the spring-damper camera the transition feels too eager, particularly visible block-to-block in a vein where the bot is otherwise standing still. Re-add the old settleDelay of 2-5 ticks pro: restores some humanness; contra: the old delay was framed as a timing buffer for the server carried-item packet, and that buffer is no longer needed since tool selection now happens during the LOOKING camera turn, so keeping the same name and timing would conflate two different reasons for the same pause. Pre-attack hesitation of 1-3 ticks under a distinct name (chosen) pro: a narrower window than the old settle, clearly labelled as humanness, with saccades starting here so the gaze trembles during the commit moment; contra: adds 50-150 ms per block break, within the authorised small reliability degradation budget. Rationale: the cleanup commit was right to remove the old delay since it solved a problem that no longer existed, but removing it entirely also removed the bit of humanness that pause was inadvertently providing. The new field reintroduces that humanness with half the duration and a clear semantic separation - tool-selection sync is handled by parallel packet sending during LOOKING, while the hesitation here is purely the human I see it, I click beat. See also [[STR-032]] and [[STR-042]].

# Problem

Which phase transitions should get a reaction delay, and why is the LOOKING to INTERACTING gate excluded?

# Lösung

Decision: a Gaussian reaction delay (mean 4 ticks, sigma 2, clamped to 1-10) is inserted at three transitions where the bot otherwise reacts instantly: SCANNING to NAVIGATING, POSITIONING to LOOKING, and INTERACTING-broken to LOOKING or next-LOOKING. The delay is not applied on the LOOKING to INTERACTING gate, which already uses the more authoritative pre-attack hesitation while the hit-result gate prevents the gate from firing too early. Alternatives: apply the reaction delay on every transition pro: most consistent humanness; contra: the LOOKING to INTERACTING gate is the latency-sensitive one for block-break timing in accelerated tests, and adding a second uncorrelated random delay on top of the pre-attack hesitation doubles the variance for no readability gain, since viewers cannot tell two short delays from one slightly longer one. No reaction delay anywhere, relying on camera smoothing pro: simplest; contra: camera smoothing only hides reaction time during a turn, and between phases - for example when the bot has already aimed and now decides to walk - there is nothing to mask the instant transition. Reaction delay only at top-of-task on SCANNING entry pro: one place to tune; contra: misses the most visible cue, the pause after a block breaks, because a bot that drops a log and instantly turns to the next log reads as a script while the pause is exactly the human notices the result moment. Reaction delay at the three chosen transitions (chosen) pro: captures the cues a viewer actually notices - decided to walk, decided to attack the next block, spotted the next block in reach - while avoiding stacking with the pre-attack hesitation; contra: the mechanism, a deferred Runnable plus a delay counter, is one extra state in the tick loop. Implementation note: the delay is realised by storing a Runnable and a tick countdown on BotController, and while the countdown is non-zero the main tick early-returns without running the current phase logic or incrementing phaseTicks, so per-phase timeouts such as navigateTimeout and lookTimeout are not eaten by the delay. releaseMovementKeys() is called when scheduling so the bot visibly stops moving during the beat instead of coasting. See also [[STR-041]] and [[STR-025]].

# Problem

Why send ServerboundSetCarriedItemPacket even when the client selected slot is already correct?

# Lösung

Decision: InventoryHelper.selectBestTool sends ServerboundSetCarriedItemPacket every time it selects a slot, even if the client-side selectedSlot is already at that index. Alternatives: setSelectedSlot only (original) pro: minimal; contra: a client-only change, so the server held-item state may diverge and break or drop calculations then use the wrong tool. Send the packet only when bestSlot differs from the current slot pro: slight bandwidth saving; contra: requires trusting that client and server are in sync, which they are not always, especially across tests. Send the packet always (chosen) pro: cheap, idempotent and guarantees server agreement; contra: one extra packet per interaction start, which is negligible. Rationale: the packet is tiny and idempotent, while a stale server-side slot is a silent-failure mode where drops are computed with the wrong tool - worth the trivial cost. See also [[STR-040]].

# Problem

Block breaks are instant and drop nothing at the start of a test - what must the test wait for after issuing gamemode survival?

# Lösung

Decision: BotTests.switchToSurvivalAt blocks on the player abilities flag, waiting until instabuild is false after issuing /gamemode survival, before the test enqueues its mining task. Alternatives: no wait (original) pro: simple; contra: racy under load - when the server has not processed /gamemode survival yet the player is still creative server-side, so block breaks are instant and drop nothing, the client receives an air update, airConfirmTicks fires, the bot moves on and no drop ever appeared. This was presented as a tool-select race for hours and was misdiagnosed. Large toolSettleTicks and airConfirmTicks values, tried pro: brute-forces timing margins; contra: does not fix the root cause, and every time system load changed the minimum safe value changed with it - 8, 16, 24 and 48 all flaked eventually. Wait on the ability-sync flag (chosen) pro: directly observes the server-to-client state actually needed, with no timing constants, eliminating the failure class rather than masking it; contra: adds a small wait, usually under one tick of wall time, and only in test setup. Hook ClientboundPlayerAbilitiesPacket via mixin pro: equivalent authoritative signal; contra: adds mixin surface for a check the existing Abilities field already exposes. Rationale: the ability-flag wait is the minimal, direct sync on the actual condition that matters. It was added after confirming the block-break-with-no-drop pattern also fired at the first mined position in walkMineWalkChop, ruling out the tool race as the sole cause. See also [[STR-030]].

# Problem

Dropped items are not always collected - why does the bot walk to an item and never pick it up?

# Lösung

Decision: tickCollecting selects the next item to walk toward by 3D distance from the player rather than horizontal-only, skips items whose absolute dy exceeds 4 blocks, and stops walking when the 3D distance drops below 1.5, the vanilla pickup radius. Alternatives: horizontal-only nearest with a 1.0-block walk stop (original) pro: simple; contra: an item 1 horizontal block away with dy=2, in the dug-out hole the bot just stood on, wins the nearest tie over an item 2 horizontal blocks away on the same Y; the bot walks to the in-hole item but its 3D distance is sqrt(5), about 2.24, which is outside the 1.5 vanilla pickup radius, so it never gets close enough - reported as dropped items are not always collected. 3D nearest with a dy filter of at most 4 and a 1.5 walk stop (chosen) pro: picks the item the bot can actually reach by horizontal walk, with the Y filter rejecting items 4 or more blocks above, unreachable without climbing, or below, past safe-fall range where the bot would take fall damage chasing them, and the 1.5 stop matches the server-side pickup radius so the bot stops exactly when vanilla pickup will fire; contra: does not help items truly stuck behind walls or in water, which need A* to a reachable standoff and are addressed separately. A* path to a mesh node near the item pro: handles every reachable item including around walls; contra: requires per-tick A* and a mesh covering the item neighbourhood, and the mesh may not exist for the immediate drop area - heavier than needed for the common case. Drop tracking with a predicted final position pro: simulates the bounce and walks to the predicted resting place; contra: the server bounces drops in ways the client cannot always predict, so the precision is wasted. Rationale: 3D plus filter closes the common failure case, a drop bouncing into the bot own dug hole, with three small one-line changes, and leaves the door open to layer A* on top later for truly hard cases. See also [[STR-046]].

# Problem

How large should the item-entity search radius be in COLLECTING, given that drops bounce away from the mined block?

# Lösung

Decision: use player.getBoundingBox().inflate(8.0) for the item-entity AABB query in tickCollecting. Alternatives: 4 blocks, equal to reachDistance pro: matches mining reach; contra: drops can bounce 2-3 blocks from the mined block, so a 4-block AABB from the standoff position can miss drops 5-6 blocks away. 8 blocks (chosen) pro: covers the bounce radius; contra: in a real session it may match unrelated drops from another player. 16 blocks pro: always finds every drop; contra: larger scan cost and more false matches from nearby mobs dropping items. Rationale: 8 blocks covers the worst-case bounce while keeping the scan cheap, and the lastMinedPos walk ensures the bot actively moves toward its own drop rather than waiting passively. See also [[STR-045]].

# Problem

How does the miner behavior move the player forward without a movement task, and why does it never press movement keys itself?

# Lösung

Decision: the behavior never explicitly moves the player. It plans the next dig batch and relies on the existing task-layer movement - drops from the freshly dug step pull the player forward via the COLLECTING walk-to-drop, and any target that ends up out of reach is closed by the controller SCANNING and POSITIONING phases when its task starts. Alternatives: a new MoveToTask task type pro: explicit control over the player position; contra: the whole task pipeline - LOOKING and INTERACTING gates, break confirmation, collect - is built around block interaction, so a movement-only task would need special-casing in nearly every controller phase. Behavior presses movement keys directly pro: no bot-module change; contra: breaks the layering contract, since two systems driving input simultaneously is exactly the failure mode the behavior layer exists to prevent. Ride the collect-walk plus positioning (chosen) pro: zero new mechanics, and the forward drift is the natural step into the space you just dug to pick up the drops that a human shows, while POSITIONING already covers the out-of-reach fallback with or without a mesh; contra: advancement is indirect, so if a slice yields no drops the player only catches up when the next task goes out of reach, 1-2 slices later - acceptable because reach is 4 while slices advance 1. Rationale: riding the existing movement was chosen because every alternative adds a parallel movement path that can fight the human-like one already tuned in the task layer. See also [[STR-024]].

# Problem

Should the strip miner handle hazards like lava and caves, or abort the run?

# Lösung

Decision: liquids ahead or overhead, bedrock in the dig path, a missing floor and open caves abort the run with a reason (FAILED plus a status line). Only two soft cases exist: a single-slice air pocket is tunneled through, and an unreachable or blocked ore is skipped via a remembered skip-set. Alternatives: handle hazards by placing blocks against lava, bridging holes and lighting caves pro: autonomous long sessions; contra: requires block placement, inventory management and a USE interaction path, none of which the task layer has yet - each is its own project, and bolting naive versions on risks drowning the bot in lava on the first edge case. Ignore hazards pro: simplest; contra: the bot walks into lava at diamond level, the single most common way to lose a session. Fail fast with a reason (chosen) pro: the dangerous cases become clean, explainable stops so the user repositions and restarts, matching the project authoritative state over hope testing philosophy; contra: runs end early in hazardous terrain. Skip and reroute around hazards pro: keeps mining; contra: re-planning the tunnel line around obstacles is real pathfinding through unmined volume, out of scope for v1 and partially covered anyway by restarting in a new direction. Rationale: fail-fast was chosen because the cost of a wrong hazard guess, lava, is total while the cost of a clean stop is one chat message. The ore skip is the exception because a single unreachable ore is local, harmless, and should not kill an hour-long run.

# Problem

How is an ore next to the tunnel acquired, and why did the thin line-of-sight approach fail?

# Lösung

Decision: oreScanRadius defaults to mining reach (4). A found ore is acquired by digging a 4-connected line of 1x2 columns, foot plus head at tunnel height, from the player column to the ore column, then the ore itself. Ores from one below the gallery floor, mined from above, to one above its ceiling, mined from below, are reachable; out-of-layer ores and galleries crossing bedrock or liquid go to the skip-set. Every planned block is recorded in an excavated set so the tunnel cave check never mistakes the run own galleries for natural caves. Alternatives: thin eye-to-ore line-of-sight exposure (first attempt) pro: fewest blocks; contra: failed in practice, because the line is computed from the planning position but deeper line blocks stay hidden behind the still-solid foot blocks, so the hit-result gate raycast lands on the blocker - 18 look timeouts in one test run - and the player cannot follow a non-walkable pinhole; its diggings also turned future tunnel slices to air, which the cave check then mis-read as cave ahead and failed the run. Large scan radius plus navigate to the ore pro: finds more diamonds per tunnel; contra: navigation needs mesh nodes, which do not exist inside solid rock, so reaching distant ore means excavating access tunnels, a planning problem far beyond v1, and it drags the bot away from the protected tunnel into unchecked terrain. Walkable 1x2 gallery plus excavated set (chosen) pro: each column is frontally visible from the previous one and the collect-walk pulls the player in after every block, so the hit-result gate always sees its target up close; 4-connected with one axis step per column because a diagonal line leaves corner walls the player cannot pass; and the excavated set cleanly separates our air from cave air; contra: roughly twice the blocks of a thin line, and it misses ore more than about 4 blocks off the tunnel and outside the 4 reachable layers - by design, since strip-mining density comes from tunnel length. Mine a 1x1 access shaft to each ore pro: reaches anything; contra: leaves the floor and ceiling riddled with holes the collect-walk can fall into, and is not walkable, with the same visibility problem as the thin line. Rationale: the gallery was chosen because the thin-line variant demonstrably fails on the two mechanics everything else relies on, hit-result visibility and collect-walk advancement, while the gallery rides exactly those mechanics - it is the shape a human digs to an ore spotted in the wall. See also [[STR-050]] and [[STR-051]].

# Problem
